column3: Uses al-A'la for Moses in a reassurance that contrasts Pharaoh's public self-exaltation.
Frames the making of many gods into one deity, a parallel challenge to exclusive lordship claims.
Places true exaltation beyond what people say, directly countering the claimed supreme status.
Joins Rabb and al-A'la as a divine designation, directly contrasting Pharaoh's appropriation.
Records Pharaoh's denial and disobedience immediately before the proclamation.
Uses al-A'la for the highest horizon, supporting a non-political register for exaltation.
Shares a speech formula only; its individual utterance does not clarify lordship.
Records the gathering and call that stage the proclamation as a public political act.
Shows Pharaoh's council publicly characterizing Moses, supplying a courtly setting for competing claims.
Assigns Rabb to Allah across generations, directly opposing Pharaoh's claim over his people.
Names a group as transgressors after loss, resonating with the tyrant's excess without fixing the referent.
Uses highness for a garden; it supplies only a distinct spatial use of the root.
Uses Rabb al-A'la for the true object of seeking, contrasting the claimant's self-directed supremacy.
Supplies the punitive aftermath, framing the proclamation within accountability rather than validated rule.
Names Allah Rabb al-alamin in praise, a broad counterpoint without the proclamation's political setting.
Uses al-A'la for the exalted assembly, distinguishing that phrase from Pharaoh's self-description.
Identifies Pharaoh as having transgressed, establishing the narrative judgment behind his claim.
Invokes the Rabb of revelation; it offers general divine authority but no close dispute.
A public 'he said' labels a sign as inherited magic, paralleling hostile interpretive speech rather than lordship.
Shows an elite defending its gods, a secondary parallel for collective resistance to exclusive divine authority.
Addresses people through their Rabb and the Hour; only a general contrast to human lordship.
Presents a speaker's self-comparative wealth and followers, a limited parallel to boastful self-ranking.
Begins Moses' invitation to purification, the immediate counter-movement to Pharaoh's later assertion.
Uses Rabb in devotional petition; it does not illuminate the contested claim.
Contrasts guidance from the Rabb with a speaker disclaiming guardianship, only indirectly relevant.
No clear lexical or narrative contribution to the proclamation.
Names Allah Rabb al-alamin, a foundational counterpoint to Pharaoh's claimed lordship over an audience.
Locates truth with the Rabb and denies prophetic agency over others, a broad authority contrast.
Offers guidance to Pharaoh toward his Rabb, directly opposing his later self-ascription of rabbhood.
Shows creatures acting by command and not preceding speech; no close relation to the claim.
A messenger's warning speech before punishment offers only a loose narrative parallel.
No clear lexical or narrative contribution to the proclamation.
Names Allah al-Ali al-Azim over all heavens and earth, a direct cosmic counterpoint to Pharaoh's superlative.
Places truth with the Rabb and allows response; a general counterpoint, not a close parallel.
Shows Moses called by his Rabb before confronting Pharaoh, anchoring the rival authority in the sequence.
Calls the accusation human speech; only shares the speech theme.
A speaker limits the self to warning, contrasting self-presentation only at a very general level.
Pairs worldly punishment with a greater final punishment, resonating with 79:25's aftermath.
Uses the same root for Illiyyun, but in a distinct textual and eschatological sense.
A speaker disclaims expelling believers; only the first-person formula parallels.
Records Pharaoh's turning away and striving immediately before he gathers and declares.
Affirms divine oneness, a direct theological counterpoint to a human claim to ultimate lordship.
Stages the powerless confronting the arrogant after judgment, a secondary consequence-pattern for coercive rule.
States failure for one who corrupts the self, resonating with transgressive self-exaltation.
Reports a dismissive collective reply; no close lordship or Pharaoh context.
Links denial of signs to punishment and names the Rabb, but only broadly parallels the narrative.
Places the great sign before Pharaoh's denial and self-proclamation.
Names Allah as Rabb of al-Shi'ra, directly displacing any rival lordship claim.
Defines Rabb as the Lord of the audience and their forebears in Pharaoh's dispute with Moses.
No clear lexical or narrative contribution to the proclamation.
Contrasts Allah as al-Ali al-Kabir and truth with what is called besides Him as false.
Has Pharaoh ask Moses who is their Rabb, directly preceding the competing account of lordship.
Names their Rabb as fully aware; a general accountability frame only.
Forbids acting with elevation over the speaker, offering a contrary political use of the root.
A messenger identifies himself as sent by the woman's Rabb, contrasting delegated service with self-deified authority.
Names human ingratitude toward the Rabb; only a broad moral resonance.
Pairs false powers with claims that unbelievers are better guided, a secondary parallel to misdirecting authority.
A speaker goes to his Rabb for guidance, contrasting dependence on God with Pharaoh's self-sufficiency.
States Allah's greatest punishment, a consequential parallel to the punishment following Pharaoh's claim.
Rejects partners attributed to Allah and affirms His transcendence above their descriptions.
Has Pharaoh explicitly question 'Rabb al-alamin' in his exchange with Moses.
Attributes Thamud's denial to its transgression, closely resonating with Pharaoh's stated transgression.
Uses elevation for an honored station, a distinct and non-political sense.
Shares only a speech formula; no relevance to the contested claim.
Sets moral impulses in the self, only indirectly relevant to transgression.
Contrasts Iblis's arrogance with a class called al-alin, preserving distinct possible senses of elevation.
Shares only a speech formula; no relevance to lordship or exaltation.
Reports foolish speech about Allah as excessive, paralleling the evaluation of an overreaching utterance.
A petition to the Rabb for protection from devils; no close relation to Pharaoh's assertion.
Calls Pharaoh exalted in the land and excessive, directly characterizing the political form of his claim.
Uses al-mala al-a'la for an exalted assembly, a distinct celestial reading of the superlative phrase.
Names mercy from the Rabb, a general divine-authority counterpoint only.
Uses al-a'lawna for believers' assurance, a contrary communal use rather than a lordship claim.
Uses al-a'lawna for believers while discouraging weakness, another contrary non-divine use of elevation.
Reserves al-mathal al-a'la for Allah, directly distinguishing supreme attribution from Pharaoh's self-claim.
Reports one group calling another astray; only a generic hostile speech parallel.
A report introduced by 'he said'; no close authority or elevation theme.
Uses ali for an honored truthful repute, a distinct sense of elevation.
Reserves al-mathal al-a'la for Allah in heavens and earth, countering any human supreme designation.
Rejects seeking uluww in the earth, directly framing earthly self-exaltation as disapproved.
A speech of Adam's naming test; no close relation to the proclamation.
Names the speaker's Rabb after forgiveness; a general alternative relation to lordship.
A prophet petitions his Rabb; no close claim or exaltation context.
Names recompense from the Rabb, only a broad accountability resonance.
A warning speech before a promised outcome; only loosely parallels the narrative consequence.
Uses Illiyyin for the righteous record, a distinct eschatological use of the root.
A ruler's inquiry speech; no close link beyond public authority.
Forbids elevation over Allah and invokes manifest authority, a direct contrary rule for the root.
No clear lexical or narrative contribution to the proclamation.
Attributes 'our Rabb' to Allah and joins it to steadfastness, a broad counter-confession.
Those in the Fire appeal to their Rabb; only a remote accountability parallel.
Describes turning away from signs of the Rabb, broadly resonant with Pharaoh's rejection of the sign.
Pharaoh publicly declares himself better than Moses, directly paralleling his self-exalting rhetoric.
Names the Rabb as knowing corrupters; only a broad judgment frame.
Commands patience for the Rabb; no close relation to the claim.
A ruler credits his Rabb rather than himself for power, a contrary model of political authority.
A group admonishes people facing divine destruction; only a distant punishment parallel.
Names Allah as Rabb of the mighty throne, a broad divine-sovereignty counterpoint.
No clear lexical or narrative contribution to the proclamation.
Directs desire toward the Rabb, only a general alternative orientation.
Stages a ruler's rival claim over life and death, a close conceptual parallel to human appropriation of divine lordship.
Forbids taking one another as lords besides Allah, directly delimiting the relation Pharaoh claims.
Introduces Moses to Pharaoh as a messenger from Rabb al-alamin, opening the same lordship dispute.
Shows Pharaoh asserting permission over belief and threatening punishment, exposing coercive rule behind his authority.
Links Pharaoh's court, gods, and suppression of Moses' people, preserving a possible royal-cult setting.
Describes humans being taken as lords besides Allah, an important alternative form of rival lordship.
Sends Moses and Aaron with signs to Pharaoh and his chiefs, locating the proclamation within an authority contest.
Connects Pharaoh's splendor and elite wealth with leading others astray, clarifying the social reach of his rule.
Says Pharaoh led his people and that his command was not rightly guided, directly qualifying his leadership claim.
Reserves judgment and worship for Allah, a direct theological counterpoint to claimed human lordship.
Has Moses address Pharaoh concerning the signs, sustaining the contested evidentiary setting before the claim.
Commands Moses to go to Pharaoh because he has transgressed, directly framing the ruler's self-exaltation.
Repeats the commission to confront Pharaoh's transgression, reinforcing the narrative diagnosis.
Defines the true Rabb as giver of each thing's form and guidance, directly answering the rival lordship question.
Records Pharaoh's being shown signs and then denying and refusing, leading toward his proclamation.
Shows Pharaoh claiming authority to authorize belief and impose punishments, a political parallel to 79:24.
Says Pharaoh led his people astray and was not rightly guided, directly reversing his asserted authority.
Characterizes Pharaoh and his chiefs as arrogant, closely aligning with self-exalting rule.
Shows Pharaoh's elite treating Israel as their servants, supplying the domination behind the claim.
Has Pharaoh invoke having raised Moses, a direct rival use of the nurture relation carried by Rabb.
Links Pharaoh's claimed favor to enslavement, exposing coercion within his asserted benefaction.
Defines Rabb al-alamin through heavens, earth, and what lies between, directly opposing Pharaoh's bounded rule.
Extends the true Rabb's domain to east, west, and what lies between, countering local sovereign supremacy.
Records Pharaoh's threat of imprisonment, making the coercive mechanism of his authority explicit.
Again shows Pharaoh claiming prior permission over faith and threatening punishment.
Links rejection of the signs to injustice and self-exaltation, closely characterizing Pharaoh's response.
Introduces the Moses-Pharaoh account as material for a believing people, framing the proclamation's wider narrative.
Says Pharaoh sought elevation in the land, divided its people, and oppressed a group, directly interpreting earthly uluww.
Has Pharaoh deny any god for his people besides himself, the closest parallel to his claim in 79:24.
Describes Pharaoh and his forces as arrogant in the land without right, directly judging the political claim.
Ends Pharaoh and his forces in the sea, a consequence-pattern for the self-exalting regime.
Groups Pharaoh with figures who acted arrogantly in the land, preserving a wider pattern of rejected power.
Shows Pharaoh seeking to kill Moses while presenting his own rule as protection, exposing coercive counter-speech.
Has Pharaoh publicly invoke his people's present dominion, closely paralleling a sovereign proclamation to an assembled people.
Shows Pharaoh ordering a tower for access to Moses' God, extending his challenge to divine authority.
Names Pharaoh's evil course as made fair and his plotting as ruinous, qualifying his self-presentation.
Places Moses and signs before Pharaoh and his chiefs, another direct narrative route to his public claim.
Has Pharaoh proclaim the kingdom of Egypt and its rivers before his people, a close parallel sovereign address.
Says Pharaoh swayed his people and they obeyed him, clarifying the gathered audience's political susceptibility.
Characterizes Pharaoh as a humiliating oppressor and among the excessive, directly qualifying his rule.
Pairs Moses' clear authority with Pharaoh's rejection, preserving the sign-and-refusal pattern.
Recalls that warnings came to Pharaoh's people, a broader narrative counterpoint to the claim's aftermath.
Has Pharaoh's wife seek rescue from Pharaoh and his deeds, an internal contrary witness to his regime.
Includes Pharaoh among those who disobeyed a messenger and received an overwhelming seizure.
Uses Pharaoh's disobedience of a messenger as a warning precedent, preserving the rebellion-and-consequence pattern.
Invokes Pharaoh and Thamud as forces, a distant but relevant tyrannical precedent.
Names Pharaoh as possessor of the stakes, supporting a coercive-regime reading of his authority.
Says Pharaoh and comparable powers transgressed in the lands, directly aligning political dominance with excess.
